title.en: Macha Curses the Men of Ulster
title.zh: 瑪哈詛咒阿爾斯特男子

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡（納萬堡）

texts.period: Noinden Ulad tradition, medieval Irish MSS; Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), Chapter IX, eBook #52963

summary.en: The war-goddess Macha comes to Ulster as a mortal woman to help a man of the province; the Ulstermen mock her in the assembly, and her curse falls on them — at every hour of their greatest need the pains of a mother in childbirth will seize the warriors of Ulster, so that a land of heroes lies helpless, and only the boy Cuchulainn is free.
summary.zh: 戰神瑪哈化身凡女救助阿爾斯特貴族，而該省男子於集會中嘲笑於她；其詛咒隨之降臨——每逢大敵當前，阿爾斯特戰士將如臨盆之母般陣痛無力，英雄之地任敵宰割，唯少年庫丘林免於此詛。

sensitivity.note: The childbirth-curse (ces noinden Ulad) is the Táin's master-motif; in the fuller Noínden Ulad tradition Macha wins a horse-race against the king's teams while in labour, gives birth to twins, and curses — a motif tied to Irish horse-cult lore.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910: No common sickness lay upon the Province, but it came of the wrath and vengeance of the gods; for in days gone by the goddess Macha, one of the three fierce goddesses of war and battles, had visited Ulster as a mortal maid, to bring aid and comfort to one of the nobles of Ulster who was in sore distress. The king and people reviled her and brought shame and scoffing upon her, because they saw that she was not as one of themselves; they made game of her in the public assembly, crowding round her, scoffing at her courage and splendid form and at her swiftness of running beyond any of the men — for they knew not that she was one of the great gods. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Then Macha cursed the men of Ulster and told them that in a time of danger and sore need, when all the chiefs and warriors of Ireland should gather round its borders, plundering and destroying, she would cast upon their warriors weakness and feebleness of body and of mind, so that they could not go forth in defence of the Province, and the land should be a prey to their enemies. Only upon Cuchulainn she laid not her curse, for he was young; and it fell not upon women and little children, but upon full-grown warriors only, because it was the men of Ulster who had insulted her. In dread of her they called the king's palace Emain Macha, the Brooch-pin of Macha, to this day. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. IX; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, London 1910 (public domain); underlying: Noinden Ulad (Ces Ulad), ed. and trans. Whitley Stokes and Kuno Meyer, Revue Celtique XI (1890), public domain

narrative.en:
The Táin Bó Cúailnge is only possible because of a woman the men of Ulster insulted; this tale, the Noínden Ulad or 'the Debility of the Ulstermen', is the fore-tale that switches off a whole heroic race.

Macha — one of the three war-goddesses, with Badb and the Morrígan — came to Ulster in the old days as a mortal maid, to bring aid and comfort to one of the nobles of the province who was in sore distress. Her origin is the otherworld: in the fuller versions she is the wife of Crunnchu, blessed by the sun, and visibly pregnant with twins when the Ulstermen test her. What is certain in every version is the insult: the king and people of Ulster reviled her, because they saw that she was not as one of themselves, and because they liked not that a woman greater than themselves should take up her abode amongst them. They made game of her in the public assembly, crowding round her, scoffing at her courage and her splendid form and at her swiftness of running, which was beyond any of the men. They knew not that she was one of the great gods.

In the classic tradition she is forced to race the king's horses while the pangs of labour are on her — and she wins, throws her twins at the winning-post, and pronounces the curse: at every hour of danger, when all the warriors of Ireland gather round the borders of Ulster plundering and destroying, the men of Ulster shall be seized with the pangs of a woman in her childbed, five days and four nights, or nine nines of hours, and in that weakness the land shall be a prey to its enemies. The men laughed — then the pains took them.

Only three exemptions the goddess allowed: the women, the little children, and Cuchulainn, young enough to stand outside the age-set that had insulted her. In Hull's telling the curse is activated at the hour of Medb's invasion: the warriors of Ulster lie prostrate while Connacht marches, and the province's whole fate passes to a seventeen-year-old with a sling and a spear. The Ulstermen, in dread of her, named the king's palace for her — Emain Macha, the Brooch-pin of Macha — and the great fort of Navan in Armagh bears that name in the landscape to this day.

The tale is the Irish mirror of a universal logic: the men who abused the divine feminine are unmanned at the exact moment they need their manhood. And it is an etiology of labor — the story that teaches that the pain a woman bears in childbed is the same pain a god can lay on an army, and that armies, like mothers, can be made helpless by it.
narrative.zh: 《奪牛記》得以成立，皆因阿爾斯特男子羞辱了一位女神；本篇（Noínden Ulad，「阿爾斯特人之衰弱」）即令整個英雄種族癱瘓之前篇。瑪哈——與巴德布、摩里岡並列的三位戰神之一——昔日化身凡女救助陷入困境的阿爾斯特貴族。完整傳說中她是克倫楚之妻、受太陽祝福，受試時身懷雙胎。各版本共通者為羞辱：王與民譏辱於她，不願勝過己者為女。眾人在集會中群聚嘲弄其勇武、絕色與超越男子的奔跑。古典傳說中，她被迫於陣痛之際與王之馬隊賽跑——她勝了，於終點產下雙胎並宣讀詛咒：大敵當前時，阿爾斯特男子必染產褥之痛五日四夜，全省任敵宰割。女神僅豁免婦女、孩童與庫丘林。據赫爾之述，此詛於梅芙入侵之際生效：戰士盡臥於地，全省之命運落於一名十七歲少年。阿爾斯特人畏之，以她之名命名王宮——埃馬因·瑪哈（瑪哈之胸針）——阿馬郡納萬大堡至今仍帶此名。此故事乃普世邏輯之鏡：虐待神聖女性者，於最需陽剛之時被去勢；亦為產痛之釋義——婦女產褥之痛，神亦可加於軍隊。

functions: Master-motif of the Táin: the curse that creates the single-combat war and the boy-hero's monopoly of battle
Charter of the geis against insulting the divine feminine: national infertility as punishment
Etiology of Emain Macha's name and of the Ulster labor-pain taboo
Etiology of horse-race and twins lore: Macha's race against the king's chariot teams

region.en: Forgall's fort at Lusk (the Gardens of Lugh), Co. Dublin, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭都柏林郡盧斯克福加爾堡（魯格之花園）

texts.period: Tochmarc Emire tradition, 11th c. MSS; Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), Chapter VIII, eBook #52963

summary.en: Cuchulainn rides south in festal chariot to the Gardens of the Sun-god Lugh and courts Emer in the riddling tongue of the poets — she demands that he first prove himself in deeds — and when the year is out he scythes through her father's guards, carries her off across the Boyne, and makes the White Field the Turf of Blood.
summary.zh: 庫丘林乘節慾戰車南行至太陽神魯格之花園，以詩人隱語向艾默求愛——艾默命其先以武功證己——一年期滿，他衝過其父衛隊，越博因河帶走艾默，白野自此改稱血原。

sensitivity.note: The riddling courtship dialogue (the six gifts of womanhood; the 'shy women' riddle) is one of the most studied scenes of the Ulster cycle; Emer's challenge is the Irish equivalent of a bride-test.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910: It was on a day of the days of summer that Emer, daughter of Forgall the Wily, sat on a bench before her father's door, at his fort that is called Lusk to-day, but which in olden days men spoke of as the Gardens of the Sun-god Lugh, so sunny and so fair and fertile was that plain. Of all maids in Erin, Emer was the best, for hers were the six gifts of womanhood: the gift of loveliness, the gift of song, the gift of sweet and pleasant speech, the gift of handiwork, the gifts of wisdom and of modesty. Her father had sworn that none beneath a king or ruling prince should marry her, and any man who dared to woo her should never leave the fort alive. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Emer heard the chariot coming like thunder from the north; her sister Fiall described the two steeds like day and night, and the chariot-chief — 'gravely he looks, as though his mind revolved some serious thought, and yet a radiance as of the summer's day enfolds him round.' Emer spoke with him in the mystic ancient tongue of the bards; he claimed his strength — 'I can defend myself alone against twenty; I fear not to fight with forty; under my protection a hundred are secure; hosts fly before my name' — and named his fosterage by Conor and by the god Lugh. Emer teased him about her elder sister, then bade him go away and prove himself for a year by deeds of prowess before she would go with him as his one and only wife — and warned him that her father would try to have him killed. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: For a whole year Cuchulainn was away, and Forgall guarded the fort so well that he could not come near Emer; at the year's end he wrote a message to her on a piece of stick, and came in his war-chariot with scythes upon its wheels with a band of hardy men who entered the outer rampart and carried off Emer, striking down men on every side; Forgall followed them to the earthen outworks and fell over the rath and was taken up lifeless. They were pursued to the Boyne; Cuchulainn set Emer in a house of safety, turned and destroyed his pursuers, and the White Field was called the Turf of Blood from that day. Then he and Emer reached their home at Dun Delgan in safety, nor were they henceforth parted until death. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, London 1910 (public domain); underlying: Tochmarc Emire, ed. and trans. Whitley Stokes and Holger Pedersen, 1899 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The wooing of Emer is the Ulster cycle's courtship masterpiece — a bride-test conducted entirely in riddles, in which the poet's language is the weapon and the dowry is proof of valor.

It was on a day of the days of summer that Emer, daughter of Forgall the Wily, sat on a bench before her father's door at his fort called Lusk to-day, but which in olden days men spoke of as the Gardens of the Sun-god Lugh — so sunny and so fair and fertile was that plain, with waving meadow-grass and buttercups and may-blossom girdling the fields. Her father was a man more learned than any druid and more cunning than any man of verse, and he had sworn that no one beneath a king or ruling prince should marry her, and that any man who dared to woo her should never leave the fort alive. Of all the maids of Ireland Emer was the best, for hers were the six gifts of womanhood: loveliness, song, sweet speech, handiwork, wisdom and modesty.

Cuchulainn came south in festal chariot with Laeg before him, and the girls on the rampart watched the thunder of the two horses — one grey like day, one black like night — and the young chariot-chief, 'gravely he looks, as though his mind revolved some serious thought, and yet a radiance as of the summer's day enfolds him round.' Emer knew at once the man of whom all Ulster spoke in whispers: the boy who fought grown warriors, killed the great hound, and was foredoomed to an early death — 'this were a man to win a woman's love.'

The courtship is conducted in the mystic tongue of the poets so that the listeners understand nothing. Emer lists her own excellences — 'I was brought up in noble behaviour as every queen is reared' — and he lists his: fostered by Conor among champions and poets, kin to Lugh the Long-handed, strength to fight alone against twenty and forty, protection to a hundred. She teases him about her elder sister Fiall — 'a younger sister in Ireland may not marry before an elder' — and he answers with the oath of a man in love: not Fiall but thee. Then the bride-test: 'go away and prove yourself for a year by deeds of prowess, and then, if you come again, I will go with you as your one and only wife' — and warning: her father will try to have you killed.

The year passed in the deeds the Táin later remembers — and in the fuller sources it passes in Scáthach's school in Alba, where Cuchulainn learns the gae bolga and wins the friendship of Ferdiad, and where the woman-warrior Aife bears him a son. When the year was out Forgall had locked the fort so well that no speech could pass; Cuchulainn wrote his message to Emer on a stick of wood, and came in the war-chariot with scythes on its wheels and a band of hard men, striking down the guards on every side and carrying her off over the ramparts. Forgall followed to the earthen outworks and fell over the rath and was taken up lifeless. They were pursued to the Boyne; Cuchulainn turned at the house of safety and destroyed the pursuers along the banks, and the White Field was called the Turf of Blood from that day. Then he and Emer reached Dun Delgan in safety, nor were they henceforth parted until death — a marriage that will be tested by fairy women, by queens, and by the whole luck of the cycle.
narrative.zh: 艾默求婚記乃阿爾斯特故事圈之求愛傑作——全程以謎語行聘禮之試，詩人之語言即兵器，嫁妝即武功之證。夏日之一日，狡詐者福加爾之女艾默坐在其父堡門前之長凳——該堡今日稱盧斯克，古時人稱太陽神魯格之花園——草原微波、毛茛金黃、山楂花環野。其父比任何德魯伊更博學、比任何詩人更狡黠，曾立誓：非王侯不得娶其女；凡敢求愛者必不得生離此堡。全愛爾蘭少女中以艾默為最，蓋其具婦女六藝：美、歌、慧言、手工、智、謙。庫丘林乘節慾戰車南來，萊格御於前，牆上少女聞雙馬之雷——一灰如晝、一黑如夜。求婚全以詩人隱語行之，旁人不解。艾默列其美德，他列其技：科恩王所養、魯格長手之親、可獨抗二十、不懼四十。她以其姊菲亞爾戲之——『愛爾蘭幼女不得先於長女嫁』——他以戀人之誓答之：非菲亞爾，是爾。繼而聘禮之試：『去以武功證己一年，再來時，我將為你唯一之妻』——並警告其父將殺你。此年為斯卡哈學校之年：庫丘林習得gae bolga、結識弗迪亞、女戰士艾菲為其生子。年期一滿，庫丘林以木棍書信傳予艾默，乘刃輪戰車率剛勇一隊而至，遍擊衛兵、越牆奪艾默。福加爾追至外土工事、跌落塹壕而死。眾追至博因河；庫丘林回身毀滅追兵，白野自此改稱血原。二人安然抵敦·德爾岡之家，至死不分離。

title.en: The Carving of Mac Dathó's Pig

region.en: The Hostel of Mac Dathó, Leinster (near Naas, Co. Kildare), Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基爾代爾郡納斯附近麥克·達霍客棧

texts.period: Recorded in the Book of Leinster, c. 1160 (TCD MS 1339); Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume I (1905), 'The Carving of Mac Dathó's Pig', eBook #5678

summary.en: Mac Dathó of Leinster promises his marvelous hound Ailbe to both Ulster and Connacht, so that both armies arrive on the same day; over a seven-year pig fed on the milk of fifty cows, the champions compete for the champion's portion — Ket puts the whole of Ulster to shame until Conall arrives — and the feast ends in a battle in which the house is ruined and the hound chooses his side.
summary.zh: 萊因斯特的麥克·達霍將神犬艾爾貝同時許給阿爾斯特與康諾特，致兩軍同日抵達；宴上以五十牛乳所養巨豬爭『勇士之份』——康特羞辱阿爾斯特全軍，直至科納爾到場——宴終於大戰，客棧被毀，神犬自擇其主。

sensitivity.note: The champion's portion contest is one of the defining institutions of the Ulster cycle; the tale is preserved complete only in the Book of Leinster.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: Mac Datho of Leinster had a hound named Ailbe that guarded the whole of Leinster, and messengers came from both Ailill and Medb of Connacht and from Conor of Ulster asking for it, each offering treasures and cattle and a third of their realm. His wife's counsel ended his fasting misery: 'Of that hound to them both be thou giver, and who dies for it little we care.' He promised it to both provinces and arranged that both armies should arrive on the same day; the house had seven doors and fifty couches between each two doors, and it was no meeting of friends that was then seen in that house. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: They slaughtered Mac Dathó's boar, nurtured seven years upon the milk of fifty cows; Bricriu called from above that the only test of division was the champion's portion: 'surely each man of you hath struck the other a buffet on the nose ere now!' Ket son of Maga rose above all the men of Ireland, hung his weapons higher than any, took a knife and stood at the boar: 'Find ye now one man among the men of Ireland who can equal my renown.' He put down Laegaire (pierced through in a border-raid), Angus son of Lama Gabaid (he had cut his father's hand off), Eogan (he had torn out one of his eyes), Munremur (the midmost of three heads he had taken was his firstborn son's), Mend the Sword-heeled (he had made his father's nickname by cutting off his heel), Celtchar (his spear had diseased him in leg and groin), and Cuscrid the Stammerer (whose first trial of arms had cost the third part of his folk and the sinews of his neck) — and the whole province of Ulster sat down before him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Conall the Victorious entered the hall, and his claim was only this: 'I have seldom slept without the head of a slain man of Connaught as my pillow; and I have not let pass a day or a night in which a man of Connaught hath not fallen by my hand.' 'Thou art a better warrior than I,' said Ket; 'were but Anluan here!' 'Aye, but Anluan is here!' cried Conall, and plucked Anluan's head from his belt and threw it at Ket, so that its blood was dashed over his lips. Ket came away from the boar, and Conall took the tail, a load for nine men, and sucked it all into his mouth; to the men of Connaught he gave only the two fore-legs, and both hosts sprang up — the heap of bodies inside the house rose as high as its side-walls, blood flowed under the doors, Fergus tore up an oak-tree by the roots, and the battle went on outside, where Mac Dathó loosed the hound to see to which side its sense would turn; and the hound joined the men of Ulster, and rushed on the defeated Connachtmen. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. I, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Scéla Mucce Meic Dathó, ed. Rudolf Thurneysen, 1910 (from Book of Leinster, TCD MS 1339)

narrative.en:
The pig-tale is the Ulster cycle's comic epic of the champion's portion — a duel of curriculum vitae conducted across a table, ending in architecture ruined by reputation.

Mac Dathó of Leinster kept a hound named Ailbe that guarded the whole of Leinster; messengers came to him from both Ailill and Medb of Connacht and from Conor of Ulster, each offering treasures, cattle, and a third of their realm for the dog. Mac Datho ate nothing and slept not, and his wife's verses solved the impasse: give the hound to them both, 'and who dies for it little we care.' So both armies were promised the same dog on the same day — and the house that received them had seven doors and fifty couches between each pair, for it was no meeting of friends: for three hundred years before the birth of Christ there had been war between Ulster and Connacht.

The feast-piece was Mac Dathó's boar, fed seven years on the milk of fifty cows, an animal so vast and so poisoned with enmity that many of the men of Ireland would die for it. Bricriu, from above, announced the law of the feast: there can be but one test of division, the champion's portion — 'surely each man of you hath struck the other a buffet on the nose ere now!' Then Ket son of Maga of Connacht rose above every man of Ireland, hung his weapons at a greater height than any, and took the knife: 'Find ye now one man among the men of Ireland who can equal my renown.' And he worked the hall like an advocate, undressing Ulster's heroes one by one: Laegaire the Triumphant who fled a border-raid pierced through with a spear; Angus son of Lama Gabaid, whose father's hand Ket had cut off with his own spear; Eogan of Fernmay, whose eye Ket had torn out; Munremur, whose firstborn's head Ket had taken; Mend, whose father's nickname (the Sword-heeled) was Ket's own work; Celtchar, diseased in leg and groin by Ket's spear; Cuscrid the Stammerer, whose first trial of arms had cost the third of his folk and the sinews of his neck. The whole province sat down.

Into that silence walked Conall the Victorious, straight from a raid, and his claim was one sentence: 'I have seldom slept without the head of a slain man of Connaught as my pillow, and I have not let pass a day or a night in which a man of Connaught hath not fallen by my hand.' Ket conceded the point — 'thou art a better warrior than I; were but Anluan here!' — 'Aye, but Anluan is here!' cried Conall, and plucked Anluan's head from his belt and threw it at Ket's chest so that the blood dashed over his lips. Conall took the boar's tail — a load for nine men — and sucked it into his mouth, and to Connacht he gave only the two fore-legs; and the hall exploded. The heap of bodies inside the house rose as high as its side-walls; blood flowed under the doors strong enough to drive a mill; Fergus tore up a great oak-tree by the roots; and the battle burst through the seven doors into the court. Outside, Mac Dathó loosed Ailbe to see which side the dog's sense would turn — and the hound joined the men of Ulster and rushed on the defeated Connachtmen, seizing the chariot-poles of Ailill and Medb at the ford that still bears the hound's name. The trick that ended in neither host gaining a dog, and in a hall's worth of champions dead of a division, is the Irish lawbook of status: worth is measured, in this world, in heads.
narrative.zh: 豬之分割記乃阿爾斯特故事圈中『勇士之份』的滑稽史詩——一場跨桌而行的履歷決鬥，終以名譽毀掉建築。萊因斯特的麥克·達霍畜神犬艾爾貝守護全萊因斯特；康諾特之艾利爾與梅芙、阿爾斯特之科恩各自遣使求犬，各許珍寶牛群與其地三分之一。麥克·達霍之妻以詩解困：『犬予兩家，死與否，吾等何懼。』兩軍遂約同日取犬——大屋有七門、每兩門之間五十張臥榻，蓋此聚非友朋之會。宴上主菜為五十牛乳養育七年之巨豬，巨而含毒，致愛爾蘭多人將為其死。布里克魯自高處宣布宴法：分割惟一之試，即勇士之份。康特·馬加之子於全場之上站起、執刀立於豬旁：『愛爾蘭可有聲名堪與我比者？』他如訟師逐一剝去阿爾斯特英雄之譽——萊加雷（邊境之戰中帶矛傷而逃）、安古斯（其父之手為康特之矛所斷）、伊奧甘（一目為康特所挖）、蒙雷穆爾（其長子之頭為康特所得）、劍踵者門德（其父之綽號乃康特斷其踵所贈）、克爾特查爾（腿股為康特之矛所傷致疾）、結巴者庫斯克里德（首試兵器即失三分之一族人、頸筋被斷）。全省之人皆坐。沉默中，科納爾·維克托里奧蘇斯直入大廳，其聲名僅一句：『自持矛以來，我幾無一夜不以康諾特人之頭為枕，無一日一夜無康諾特人死於我手。』康特讓之——『若安魯安在此！』——『安魯安在此！』科納爾自腰帶拔安魯安之頭擲於康特胸前，血濺其唇。科納爾取九人方可抬之豬尾全數吸入口中；予康諾特者僅前足兩條。大廳即時炸裂：屍堆高及牆垣、血自門下流洩、弗格斯連根拔起橡樹、戰鬥衝出七門。院外麥克·達霍放出艾爾貝——犬遂投阿爾斯特人，撲向敗逃之康諾特軍。詭計終局：兩軍皆未得犬，而一廳之英雄死於一場分割——此世之價值，以頭顱計量。

title.en: The Sick-Bed of Cuchulainn and Fand the Tear of Beauty
title.zh: 庫丘林病榻與美之淚芬德

region.en: Tete Brecc (the Sick-Bed), Emain Macha, Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡特特·布雷克（病榻之所）

texts.period: Recorded in Leabhar na hUidre, c. 1100 (transcribed by Maelmuiri mac Ceileachair); Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume I (1905), 'The Sick-Bed of Cuchulain', eBook #5678

summary.en: Two birds linked by a chain of red gold lull the men of Ulster asleep at Samhain and put Cuchulainn into a year's sick-bed; from the Plain of Delight, Liban brings Fand — Manannan's released wife, whose beauty is compared only to a tear — to offer her love for a day's battle; Emer comes whetting knives, and Manannan shakes his cloak between the lovers, while the Druids give both husband and wife a drink of forgetfulness.
summary.zh: 薩溫之夜，紅金鏈相連之雙鳥使阿爾斯特男子入睡，並使庫丘林臥病一年；自宜人平原，莉班攜芬德——瑪南南已釋之妻，其美僅可比淚——以一日之戰事易其情愛；艾默攜磨利之刀而來；瑪南南於二情侶之間搖其斗篷，德魯伊則予夫妻二人遺忘之飲。

sensitivity.note: Fand ('tear') is Manannan's ex-wife in this tale; her resignation scene is one of the great love-debates of medieval literature. Retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: At the Samhain festival on the Plain of Murthemne, two birds flying over the lake, linked together by a chain of red gold, sang a gentle song and a sleep fell upon all the men; Cuchulainn rose to pursue them, missed with stone and spear until the spear pierced the shield of the wing of one, and the birds went beneath the lake. He leaned his back against a pillar and a sleep fell on him; two women came to him in turn, one in a green mantle and one in a purple folded in five folds, laughing and striking him with a horsewhip until he was all but dead. For a year he lay speechless on the sick-bed at Tete Brecc, until Angus son of Aed Abra sang to the Ulstermen of the healing that Liban and Fand would bring. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Liban, from her spouse Labraid the Swift, Sword-Wielder, offered Cuchulainn Fand, daughter of Aed Abra, whose husband Manannan the Son of the Sea had released her, in exchange for one day's service in battle against Senach the Unearthly, Eochaid Juil and Yeogan the Stream. Fand is the name of the tear that runs from the eye — nothing in the world but a tear to which her beauty could be likened. Cuchulainn rose, fought the day's battle alone against three thousands in the otherworld's plain, and slept with the lady for a month; they made tryst at the Strand of the Yew-Tree's Head. Emer came there with fifty women and knives whetted to slay the lady, and found Cuchulainn and Laeg at chess. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Emer rebuked Cuchulainn before the women of Ulster, and he answered that Fand was fair and skilled and wealthy; Emer replied that the lady was in no way better than herself — 'fair seems all that's red; seems white what's new alone; and bright what's set o'erhead; and sour are things well known! Men worship what they lack; and what they have seems weak.' Fand resigned him: 'Emer! noble lady! Take thy man to thee; though my arms resign him, longing lives in me.' Manannan perceived her unequal war, came riding the maned waves of the sea, and asked whether she would go or stay; she chose Manannan — 'he hath no consort equal to himself, but Cuchulainn hath already.' Cuchulainn leaped three times into the air and made three leaps south to Tara Luachra, where he lay without meat or drink; the Druids bound him and gave him a drink of forgetfulness, and Emer one for her jealousy, and Manannan shook his cloak between Cuchulainn and Fand so that they might never meet again throughout eternity. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. I, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Serglige Con Culainn (older edition: Windisch, Irische Texte I, 1870, public domain)

narrative.en:
The Sick-Bed of Cuchulainn is the Ulster cycle's answer to the Táin: after the epic of war, an epic of love, in which the hero of the ford is undone by a woman's tear.

Every year at Samhain the men of Ulster held festival on the Plain of Murthemne, where each man declared his combats, carrying in a pouch the tips of the tongues of the foes he had killed — and swords laid over thighs turned on any man who lied. Two birds came over the lake linked by a chain of red gold, singing a gentle song that put the whole assembly to sleep. Cuchulainn rose to hunt them, missed with stone and sling and spear until the spear went through the shield of the wing of one; the birds sang again and went beneath the lake, and a sleep fell on him. Two women appeared in turn — one in a green mantle, one in purple folded five-fold — and each struck him laughing with a horse-whip until he was all but dead. They left; a year he lay without speech on the sick-bed at Tete Brecc, refusing Emer's Dun Delga.

At the year's end the man Angus son of Aed Abra sang the diagnosis from the doorway: the women of the Sídhe had put their power on him, and healing lay in the Plain of Delight. At the pillar stone Liban appeared — wife of Labraid the Swift, Sword-Wielder — with an offer: Fand, daughter of Aed Abra, Manannan the Son of the Sea's released wife, for one day's battle against Senach the Unearthly, Eochaid Juil and Yeogan the Stream. Fand is the tear that runs from the eye; nothing in the world but a tear could her beauty be likened to. Laeg was carried across on the woman's shoulder to see the island of thrice-fifty couches and thrice-fifty welcome-song women.

Cuchulainn rose from the sick-bed like a man waking from death, crossed to the otherworld in Liban's bronze skiff, and fought the day's battle alone against three thousands — slaying Eochaid Juil bathing at the spring, thirty-three of his men, and Senach the Unearthly in a great fight — then cooled his heat in three vats of water, the first boiling over. He slept with Fand a month; they set a tryst at the Strand of the Yew-Tree's Head. Emer heard of it and came there with fifty women and knives whetted for the fairy's death, and found Cuchulainn and Laeg at chess. Fand saw the gold clasps and the green-edged knives first. Cuchulainn defended them both with a boast — but Emer answered with the most famous speech in the cycle, the truth of desire: 'Fair seems all that's red; seems white what's new alone; and bright what's set o'erhead; and sour are things well known! Men worship what they lack; and what they have seems weak.'

Fand released him with the grace of a queen: 'Emer, noble lady, take thy man to thee; though my arms resign him, longing lives in me.' Manannan, riding the maned waves of the sea where no vessel was needed, perceived his wife's unequal war, and asked her which she would do; she chose him, for Cuchulainn had a wife already and she none. As she went, Manannan shook his cloak between the mortal and the immortal so that they might never meet again throughout eternity. The Druids of Ulster hunted down the maddened hero in the mountains of Tara Luachra, bound him with fairy songs, and gave him — and gave Emer, for her jealousy was no better than his sickness — a drink of forgetfulness. So ends the cycle's one romance: with pharmaceutical forgetting standing in for mercy, and a god's cloak for a wall that time cannot build.
narrative.zh: 《庫丘林病榻》乃阿爾斯特故事圈對《奪牛記》之回應：戰爭史詩之後是愛之史詩——渡口英雄竟被一女子之淚擊倒。每年薩溫之夜，阿爾斯特男子在穆爾西姆尼平原集會驗功、袋中攜所殺之敵之舌尖——劍橫於腿上，誰若說謊，劍即反噬。紅金鏈相連之雙鳥飛過湖上、歌聲使全場入睡。庫丘林追之不中、矛貫其一鳥翼上之盾；雙鳥潛入湖底，睡意臨於英雄之身。兩女子輪流以馬鞭擊之至其垂死。此後一年，他臥於特特·布雷克病榻、不言不語。歲末，安古斯自門口唱出診斷：西德之女施加其力於他，愈病之方在宜人平原。石柱旁莉班現身獻議：芬德——瑪南南已釋之妻——以一日之戰相易。芬德者，眼中所流之淚也；其美惟淚可喻。庫丘林如死而復甦者起身、乘銅舟渡往彼岸，獨戰三千、殺敵而歸，於三缸水中冷卻其熱。與芬德同眠一月，相約紫杉首灘。艾默攜五十女子與磨利之刀而來，庫丘林與萊格正弈棋。艾默答以全圈最著名之言、慾望之真諦：『赤者看似美；新者看似白；高懸者看似亮；習見者轉為酸！人皆崇拜其所未有；所有者似弱。』芬德以女王之風讓之：『艾默，貴女，取回爾之男子；我雖放開雙臂，思念長存於我。』騎乘鬃浪之瑪南南問其去留；她擇瑪南南——因庫丘林有妻、而她無夫。瑪南南於凡人與不朽者之間搖其斗篷，使二人永世不得再會。德魯伊於塔拉·盧阿克拉斯山縛住瘋癲之英雄，予他——亦予艾默——遺忘之飲。全圈唯一戀曲如此終結：以遺忘代替慈悲，以神之斗篷代替時間不能築起之牆。

title.en: Deirdre and the Sons of Usnach
title.zh: 德爾德麗與烏斯納之子

region.en: Emain Macha (Navan Fort), Co. Armagh, Northern Ireland
region.zh: 北愛爾蘭阿馬郡埃馬因·瑪哈堡（納萬堡）

texts.period: Longes mac nUisnenn, Book of Leinster and Glenn Masain versions, 11th-15th c.; Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume I (1905), 'The Exile of the Sons of Usnach', eBook #5678

summary.en: A baby cries in its mother's womb at a feast and Cathbad the druid names her Deirdre, the cause of ruin; the king rears her in seclusion to wed her, but she sees a raven drinking blood on snow and will love only the man with those three colors — Naisi, whom she seizes by the ears until he flees with her to Alba — until treachery brings the three brothers home and the whole Red Branch burns.
summary.zh: 宴上嬰兒於母腹中啼叫，德魯伊卡斯巴德命名其為德爾德麗——毀滅之因；王幽禁撫養欲娶之，她卻見烏鴉於雪上飲血，言必愛具此三色者——烏斯納之子奈西——她扯其耳直至兄弟攜她流亡阿爾巴；背信引三兄弟歸國，紅枝全軍化為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Deirdre ('of the Sorrows') is the Helen of the Ulster cycle; the exiles' burning of Emain is historical for the cycle's chronology. Retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: In the house of Feidlimid the storyteller the men of Ulster sat at their ale, and before them stood his wife, great with child; as she passed through the house the child cried out in her womb, a shriek heard through the whole house and the court without. Cathbad the druid laid his hand on her and prophesied: a fair maid with blue-centred eyes and cheeks like the foxglove, teeth faultless and lips like coral, for whose love many chiefs shall strive — 'Deirdre shall be her name, and evil woe shall be upon her... Usna's sons, the three chiefs sublime, to banishment forced shall be.' The young men cried 'Let that maiden be slain!'; but Conor said she should be reared to be his wife. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Deirdre was reared in a house of Conor's far from the court, seen by no man but her foster-father, foster-mother and Levorcham the witch. One winter day the calf's blood lay on the snow and a raven came down to drink it: 'That man only will I love who hath the three colours that I see here, his hair as black as the raven, his cheeks red like the blood, and his body as white as the snow.' Levorcham named Naisi the son of Usnach. Deirdre escaped to Emain's rampart where Naisi stood alone; he refused for fear of Cathbad's prophecy, she seized him by the two ears — 'Two ears of shame and of mockery shalt thou have if thou take me not with thee' — and Naisi, his brothers and thrice-fifty warriors went with her into exile in Alba. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: At last Conor offered protection and Fergus, Dubhtach and Cormac as sureties; Fergus was delayed by an ale-feast contrived by Conor, and the three brothers, pledged to eat no food in Erin until they had eaten of Conor's, went on to the meadows of Emain. Eogan of Fernmay — whose peace Conor had just made — drove his spear through Naisi's back; Fiacha son of Fergus shielded Naisi with his body and died over him; there was murder through the meadow, Dubhtach slew Conor's son and daughter, and Fergus burned Emain before dawn. Deirdre lived a year in Conor's house smiling never, singing that sweeter than Conor's mead was the foam of the waterfall, more magic than horns and pipes the voice of Usna's sons; then — in the later Glenn Masain version Hull follows — she leapt from the chariot on the field and broke her head on the stones, and from her grave and Naisi's on either side of the loch two pines grew and entwined across the water until King Conor died. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905 and Hull 1910; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. I, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Longes mac nUisnenn (Book of Leinster version, ed. Whitley Stokes, 1902, public domain); Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

narrative.en:
Deirdre is the Ulster cycle's Helen and Cassandra at once — desired for a beauty druids read in her mother's womb, and fated to be the ruin of a kingdom that never once asks her consent.

In the house of Feidlimid son of Dall, Conor's storyteller, the men of Ulster sat at their ale; before them stood Feidlimid's wife, great with child. As she crossed the floor, the child cried out in her womb — a shriek that filled house and court — and Cathbad the druid laid his hand on her and read the future aloud: a fair maid with blue-centred eyes, cheeks like the foxglove, teeth faultless, lips like coral, for whose love many chiefs shall strive; her name shall be Deirdre, and evil woe shall be upon her: Usna's three sons forced to banishment; Fergus to exile; a son of Conor dead; a grim deed in wrath against the king of Ulster — and her own tiny grave. The young men cried 'Let that maiden be slain!' But Conor answered that she should be brought to him in the morning, reared to his will, and be his wife — the fated girl converted into the king's property.

She was reared in a house far from the court, seen of no man but her foster-father and foster-mother and Levorcham the witch, whom none could refuse. One winter day her foster-father skinned a calf on the snow to make her a roast; the blood lay red on the white, and a black raven came down to drink it. 'That man only will I love,' said Deirdre, 'who hath the three colours that I see here — his hair as black as the raven, his cheeks red like the blood, and his body as white as the snow.' Levorcham answered that such a man was near: Naisi, son of Usnach. Deirdre went out to the rampart of Emain where Naisi stood alone; he refused her for fear of Cathbad's prophecy — and she sprang on him and seized him by the two ears: 'Two ears of shame and of mockery shalt thou have if thou take me not with thee.' 'Release me, O my wife!' So they fled — three-times-fifty warriors with their women, dogs and servants — harried through Ireland, driven to the wildernesses of Alba, where they served the king in war and built themselves houses in the meadows for fear any man should see Deirdre.

The king of Alba's steward, seeing her beauty, asked her for his master; Deirdre told Naisi everything nightly. Snares and wars were set for the brothers, and they came safe out of all, until at last Conor offered protection under the surety of Fergus, Dubhtach and Cormac — sureties sacred in Irish law. Conor then contrived an ale-feast that held Fergus back, for the sons of Usnach were pledged to eat no food in Erin until they had eaten of Conor's hand. So the three walked into the meadows of Emain behind Fiacha son of Fergus, and Eogan of Fernmay — whose peace Conor had only just made — threw the spear that broke Naisi's back; Fiacha covered Naisi with his own body and died over him; murder ran through the meadow. Dubhtach slew Conor's son and daughter; three hundred of Ulster fell; and before dawn Fergus burned Emain — the Red Branch's whole glory — and went into exile with three thousand men, harrying Ulster for sixteen years.

Deirdre lived a year in Conor's house, smiling never, singing the laments whose every stanza measures Conor's court against Naisi's wilderness: sweeter than the mead of the hall, the foam of the waterfall; sweeter than horns and pipes, the voice of Usna's sons. In the Glenn Masain tradition Hull preserves, she struck her head on the stones from Conor's chariot on the field; and from her grave on one side of a loch and Naisi's on the other, two pines grew and entwined their branches across the water — and Conor would have cut them down, but the men of Ulster protected them until King Conor died. Love, in this telling, keeps growing across the king's borders after it has been killed.
narrative.zh: 德爾德麗兼具阿爾斯特故事圈之海倫與卡桑德拉：因其美貌而被覬覦——德魯伊於母腹中即讀出其美——並註定毀滅從不徵求她同意之王國。科恩之講古者費德利米德家中，阿爾斯特男子飲酒作樂；其懷孕之妻立於前，腹中嬰兒啼叫、聲滿屋院——德魯伊卡斯巴德按手讀出未來：藍心之目、狐花之頰、無瑕之齒、珊瑚之唇、群雄必爭之美女；名為德爾德麗，禍患隨之：烏斯納三子被迫流亡、弗格斯流放、科恩一子死亡、以及她自己的小小墳墓。眾青年喊『殺此女！』科恩答：按吾意撫養、為吾之妻。她被幽禁於遠離王廷之屋，除養父母與女巫萊沃坎外無男子可見。一日冬日，血紅於雪上、黑鴉落而飲之；德爾德麗曰：『我必愛具此三色之人——髮如鴉之黑、頰如血之紅、身如雪之白。』萊沃坎答：此人即烏斯納之子奈西。奈西因懼預言而拒——她抓住他雙耳：『若不帶我走，爾將有羞辱與嘲笑之雙耳。』三兄弟遂偕三九五十名戰士流亡阿爾巴荒野。阿爾巴王之總管代主求之；德爾德麗夜夜盡告奈西。直至科恩以弗格斯、達布塔赫與科爾馬克為保人賜予庇護——愛爾蘭法中神聖之保人。科恩設酒宴絆住弗格斯，因烏斯納之子曾誓：未食科恩之食不食愛爾蘭之食。甫與科恩講和之伊奧甘擲矛斷奈西之背；菲亞赫以己身護之而死；謀殺遍野、達布塔赫殺科恩之子與女、黎明前弗格斯焚埃馬因——紅枝之全部榮光——並率三千人流亡、蹂躪阿爾斯特十六年。德爾德麗居科恩家中一年、從不微笑，其哀詩每節皆以奈西之荒野衡量科恩之宮廷：比大廳蜜酒更甜者，瀑布之泡沫；比號角風笛更迷人者，烏斯納諸子之聲。格倫·馬辛傳統中，她自科恩戰車躍下、頭觸石而碎；其墓與奈西墓隔湖相對，兩株松樹自墓中生出、枝椏隔水相纏——科恩欲斬之，而阿爾斯特男子護之直至王死。愛，在被殺之後仍跨過國王之疆界繼續生長。

variants.name: Glenn Masain version
variants.summary: Adds Deirdre as seer, the whale's blood feast of Naisi's dream, and her death from Conor's chariot — the romantic ending adopted by Hull and most retellings.
